newsitem.title: USA: Wachovia targets high-growth area with deal.
newsitem.headline: Wachovia targets high-growth area with deal.

text.p: After a six-year hiatus, Wachovia Corp returned to the acquisition game on Tuesday with a $542 million transaction that would greatly expand its presence in the growing Virginia market.

The agreed purchase of Jefferson Bankshares Inc would expand a 20-year relationship between the two banks and also would reunite Jefferson chief executive Kenton McCartney, who left Wachovia in 1984, with his former employer.
"It's a very attractive deal for Wachovia and everyone else concerned," said John Mason of Interstate/Johnson Lane.
Wachovia earlier said it would buy Jefferson in a stock transaction that values shares of Jefferson at $38.83 based on Monday's closing stock price.
Shares of Jefferson surged 8 to 38 in midday trading, while Wachovia stock gained 3/8 to 62-1/2.
Officials from the banks declined to elaborate on the announcement of the transaction, saying that top executives would be available to discuss the deal later on Tuesday.
Sources who had spoken with bank officials said Jefferson, which has been a customer of Wachovia's for 20 years, made the initial approach about a transaction.
Wachovia will be paying about 2.6 times Jefferson's book value. Wall Street experts expect the deal to be finalized before the October 31 time frame set by the companies.
"The companies are very similar from a cultural standpoint," said Darren Short of Robinson-Humphrey Co Inc, who described Jefferson as "a miniature Wachovia" with a "penchant for conservatism."

Wachovia, which had kept to the sidelines in the banking merger frenzy, recently expressed interest in a Virginia expansion. Its last sizable acquisition came in 1991 when it bought South Carolina National.
Sources who spoke with the companies said the merger pact does not include a break-up fee.

About half of Jefferson's business is set in the growing areas of Richmond and Charlottesville. The transaction will double Wachovia's loan size in Virginia and significantly boost its retail operations, analysts said.
"It fits into (Wachovia's) strategy of expanding into high-growth markets in the southeast," said Cheryl Swaim of Oppenheimer & Co.
Because the acquisition of Jefferson is expected to be digested with relative ease, analysts said Wachovia soon will be able to pursue other growth prospects.
"Wachovia still retains a great deal of flexibility post this transaction," Short said.
However, analysts said it is uncertain if Wachovia intends to pursue the "super-regional" strategy being undertaken by North Carolina rivals First Union Corp and NationsBank Corp.
